title: The 4 Patterns of AI Native Development — Patrick Debois

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is on coding agents and software-engineering workflows, covering code generation, review, specification-driven development, and the developer's evolving role in the AI-in-the-IDE/PR loop. The content addresses developer platforms and coding assistants as the tools reshaping software development workflows. The four patterns span discovery, specification, development, and review phases of the software engineering lifecycle. The talk assumes familiarity with software development workflows, LLMs, RAG, MCP, and agent concepts. A conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer channel. summary: Patrick Debois introduces four AI native development patterns emerging alongside the genAI technology stack evolving from LLMs through RAG, MCP functions, agents, and early agent teams. He draws a parallel to the cloud native transition, noting we are moving from sprinkling AI on existing workflows toward genuine AI native practices where tasks get replaced, enhanced, or newly created. Pattern one, producer to manager, addresses developers shifting from writing code to managing AI agents that write code. Review time and cognitive load increase because thinking work moves into review. New review approaches include summary-based yes/no views, step-by-step multi-file review flows, and diagrammatic representations of changes. He discusses moldable development environments that adapt to the review context, autocommit heuristics (citing Adar), checkpointing for long-running agents, and setting constraints via file locks and agent permissions. Cost monitoring becomes relevant for long-running agent tasks. Pattern two, implementation to intent, moves developers from caring about implementation details to specifying intent via markdown specification files, GitHub task-oriented plans, and specification-centric workflows where functional, technical, and security requirements drive the process. Pattern three, delivery to discovery, shifts focus from production delivery to exploring what to build. Rapid prototyping tools like Lovable and Bolt enable multiple iterations and versions, and vibe coding could even let customers prototype desired interfaces. Pattern four, content creation to knowledge, involves capturing learnings from production issues, incident responses, onboarding/exit processes, feature memory, and in-flow knowledge capture where agents suggest saving important context. Debois maps these shifts to operations, QA/architecture, product ownership, and data engineering roles, noting these are what good senior developers already do. He references ainative.dev.io, which curates roughly 300 tools in the AI native dev landscape. He closes by noting the intersection of engineering and AI makes the space unique, offers to share slides via LinkedIn, and invites subscription to his YouTube channel for continued exploration.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Four AI native dev patterns: producer to manager, implementation to intent, delivery to discovery, content creation to knowledge.
Managing AI-generated code increases review burden and cognitive load; new review methods include summaries, diagrams, and step-by-step flows.
Setting constraints on agents—file locks, permissions, guardrails—mirrors how a manager sets rules for a team.
Specification files and intent-based coding shift focus from how to what; tools are becoming specification-centric rather than code-centric.
Discovery via rapid prototyping (Lovable, Bolt) enables multiple iterations; vibe coding could extend to customers prototyping interfaces.
Capturing knowledge from production issues, incidents, onboarding, and feature decisions prevents repeating problems and creates a beneficial learning loop.
The patterns map developer role shifts toward operations, QA/architecture, product ownership, and data engineering—work senior developers already do.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Debois introduces the talk, tracing genAI technology from LLMs to RAG, MCP, agents, and agent teams. He compares the current AI native transition to cloud native, noting tasks get replaced, enhanced, or newly created as developers move beyond coding and typing.

sections.title: Pattern 1: From Producer to Manager
sections.summary: Developers shift from producing code to managing AI agents that produce it. Review time and cognitive load increase. New review methods include summary views, step-by-step flows, and diagrams. Moldable development environments adapt to review context. Autocommit heuristics (Adar), checkpointing for long-running agents, constraint setting via file locks and permissions, and cost monitoring emerge as management activities.

sections.title: Pattern 2: From Implementation to Intent
sections.summary: Developers move from caring about implementation to specifying intent. Markdown specification files, GitHub task-oriented plans, and specification-centric workflows where functional, technical, and security requirements drive the process replace chat-based coding. The role shifts toward managing the specification process.

sections.title: Pattern 3: From Delivery to Discovery
sections.summary: Focus shifts from production delivery to discovering what to build. Rapid prototyping with tools like Lovable and Bolt enables multiple iterations and versions. Vibe coding can extend to customers prototyping desired interfaces, acting like A/B testing on steroids.

sections.title: Pattern 4: From Content Creation to Knowledge
sections.summary: Learning from production issues, incident responses, onboarding, feature memory, and decision tracking creates a knowledge loop. Agents can suggest saving important context in-flow, benefiting both humans and AI, and the captured knowledge helps others and improves coding.

sections.title: Summary and Resources
sections.summary: The four patterns map developer shifts toward operations (manager), QA/architecture (intent), product ownership (discovery), and data engineering (knowledge)—work senior developers already do. Debois references ainative.dev.io with roughly 300 curated tools and the AI native dev newsletter.

sections.title: Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Debois notes the intersection of engineering and AI makes the space unique, thanks the audience, offers to share slides via LinkedIn, and invites subscription to his YouTube channel for continued exploration of new ways of working.
